title: [B2 • Band 6.0] Bài 211: The Wood Wide Web: Rethinking the Subterranean Forest
passageHtml:
PASSAGE 211 (LEVEL B2 • BAND 6.0)

The Wood Wide Web: Rethinking the Subterranean Forest

Paragraph 1. For over a century, classical forestry treated trees as solitary competitors locked in a ruthless battle for sunlight, water, and nutrients. Whenever one tree absorbed moisture, foresters assumed its neighbours simply lost out. Over the past three decades, however, forest ecology has dismantled that view. Beneath leaf litter lies a dense subterranean network—widely known as the 'Wood Wide Web'—built by mycorrhizal fungi whose microscopic filaments physically link trees of different ages and species into interdependent communities.

Paragraph 2. This underground alliance rests on ancient biological trade. Trees excel at photosynthesis, producing carbon-rich sugars, yet their coarse roots struggle to extract poorly soluble minerals such as phosphorus and nitrogen from compact soil. Conversely, mycorrhizal fungi send hair-like hyphae through trillions of soil pores, delivering water and dissolved nutrients while receiving up to forty percent of the host trees' carbohydrates. 'It is neither purely generous nor purely harmful,' notes forest ecologist Dr. Suzanne Simard. 'It is a complex carbon marketplace shaped by mutual biological exchange.'

Paragraph 3. To measure resource movement across this grid, Simard designed an isotope-tracing experiment in temperate Canadian rainforests. Her team sealed branches of mature Douglas fir and paper birch trees inside airtight plastic bags and injected distinct carbon isotopes: carbon-14 and carbon-13. Instruments revealed that carbon travelled in both directions through the fungal threads. In midsummer, sunlit birch trees transferred surplus carbon to shaded fir saplings; in autumn, once leafless birch trees stopped photosynthesising, evergreen firs pumped carbon back.

Paragraph 4. Beyond sharing nutrients, the fungal web acts as a rapid warning system. Eco-physiologist Dr. Kathryn Fahy tested how broad bean plants and pine seedlings react to aphid attacks, keeping soil free of touching roots while leaving fungal threads intact. Within twenty-four hours, healthy connected plants began producing volatile defensive chemicals, such as methyl salicylate, to repel pests and summon predatory wasps. When Fahy cut the fungal connections, however, neighbouring plants received no warning and remained undefended.

Paragraph 5. Large veteran specimens called 'mother trees' anchor this subterranean grid, linking to hundreds of trees across a forest hectare. Forest geneticist Dr. Marcus Thorne showed that mother trees recognise family ties, sending noticeably more carbon and defensive compounds to their own genetic offspring than to unrelated seedlings. Yet biologists still debate how to interpret this system. Dr. Julian Kroll argues that popular media romanticises forests as caring communities, insisting fungi are opportunistic, selfish organisms trading resources only when it boosts their own survival and spore production. Thorne adds that certain parasitic plants, such as ghost pipes, even tap into the network to steal sugars without offering anything back.

Paragraph 6. These findings are reshaping modern forestry practices. Industrial clear-cutting, deep soil ploughing, and chemical fungicide sprays wipe out delicate fungal networks that took centuries to form. To prevent collapse, Simard advocates 'retention forestry', preserving veteran hub trees and undisturbed root corridors during timber harvests so newly planted seedlings can immediately plug into an active subterranean grid.

groups.title: Questions 1–4
groups.instructions: Do the following statements agree with the claims of the writer? Write YES, NO, or NOT GIVEN.

groups.title: Questions 5–8
groups.instructions:
Complete the summary using the list of words, A–G, below.

A. offspring    B. fungi    C. seasonal    D. pesticides    E. selfish    F. exchange    G. temporary
groups.template: Dr. Simard describes the underground relationship between trees and mycorrhizal fungi as a system of mutual biological 5. {{q5}} . Her Canadian fieldwork confirmed that carbon flow shifts direction according to 6. {{q6}} sunlight availability. Later studies revealed that veteran hub trees favour their own genetic 7. {{q7}} when sharing nutrients. However, Dr. Kroll cautions against overly romantic descriptions, stressing that fungi behave in a fundamentally 8. {{q8}} manner driven by their own survival.

groups.title: Questions 9–12
groups.instructions: Choose the correct letter, A, B, C or D.

q1.text: Nineteenth-century foresters already recognized that trees regularly shared nutrients underground.

steps: Đoạn 1: Hơn một thế kỷ trước, lâm nghiệp truyền thống coi cây là đối thủ đơn độc cạnh tranh khốc liệt.

q2.text: Dr. Kathryn Fahy found that pine seedlings send warning signals faster than broad bean plants.

steps: Đoạn 4: Có thử nghiệm trên cả đậu và thông, nhưng không có so sánh loài nào gửi tín hiệu nhanh hơn.

q3.text: Mature mother trees supply more carbon to their own young than to stranger seedlings.

steps: Đoạn 5: "...sending noticeably more carbon... to their own genetic offspring than to unrelated seedlings."

q4.text: Dr. Julian Kroll believes that fungi deliver nutrients between trees purely out of generosity.

steps: Đoạn 5: Dr. Kroll khẳng định nấm là sinh vật cơ hội, vị kỷ (selfish) chỉ trao đổi vì lợi ích sinh tồn của chính nó.
Đoạn 3: Mùa hè bạch dương truyền cho linh sam, mùa thu linh sam truyền lại → thay đổi theo mùa (seasonal).

q9.text: Why did Simard inject radioactive carbon isotopes into enclosed tree branches?
options: A. To kill harmful insects hiding inside tree bark
B. To measure how quickly leaves fall during autumn
C. To trace how carbon moves between two different tree species
D. To test whether plastic bags block natural sunlight

steps: Đoạn 3: Nhằm theo dõi sự di chuyển của carbon qua mạng lưới nấm giữa 2 loài cây khác nhau.

q10.text: What happened when Dr. Fahy severed the fungal threads between plants?
options: A. All plants immediately absorbed extra phosphorus from the soil.
B. Predatory wasps attacked the healthy broad bean leaves.
C. Airborne smells became twice as strong within one hour.
D. Uninfested plants received no advance warning of insect attacks.

steps: Đoạn 4: "...neighbouring plants received no warning and remained undefended."

q11.text: Why does Dr. Thorne mention ghost pipes in the fifth paragraph?
options: A. To show that some parasitic plants exploit the grid without contributing
B. To prove that fungi prefer supporting rare wildflowers over trees
C. To explain why chemical fungicides fail to kill forest weeds
D. To argue that mother trees cannot distinguish kin from strangers

steps: Đoạn 5: Ghost pipes là cây ký sinh ăn cắp đường từ mạng lưới mà không đóng góp lại gì.

q12.text: What is the primary aim of 'retention forestry' described in the final paragraph?
options: A. Replacing mixed forests with single-species timber farms
B. Leaving hub trees and root corridors intact to support young seedlings
C. Spraying soil with natural minerals before cutting down old trees
D. Removing all underground fungi prior to planting new saplings

steps: Đoạn 6: Giữ lại các cây đầu mối và hành lang rễ nguyên vẹn để cây non hòa mạng lưới ngay.
